desks.title: Pre-seed raise — $600k for Fernroom
desks.description: Raising a first round as a solo founder: the investor pipeline, the pitch narrative, the questions every investor asks, and the one meeting that decides whether the round closes.
desks.brief:
## Pre-seed raise — $600k for Fernroom

**Product** Fernroom — room and roster scheduling for allied-health clinics
**Instrument** SAFE, $6m post-money cap · **Target close** @+45d
**Use of funds** first senior engineer, 12 months of runway, 10 clinics from pilot to paid
**Runway today** 7 months, on savings and a state innovation grant

### The story in one line
Allied-health clinics lose hours every week juggling rooms and rosters; Fernroom makes the schedule fix itself.

### Traction to lead with
- 6 pilot clinics, 4 now paying $149 a month
- 31 discovery calls across two rounds — pricing evidence is on the discovery desk
- More than 80% of pilot staff use it every week

### Where it stands
$175k committed from 3 angels. **The Wattle Seed Fund partner meeting @+3d is the one that moves the round** — a $250k lead plus the syndicate's $100k takes it to $525k and gives the undecided angels a reason to decide.

callout.title: The meeting that moves the round
callout.body: Wattle Seed Fund partner meeting @+3d. A $250k lead plus the syndicate's $100k takes the round to $525k of $600k. Rehearse the traction slide twice, and bring the two-tier pricing from the discovery desk — they will ask.

rows.investor: Priya — angel, ran a clinic group

children.label: Hours lost to rosters every week
Live walk-through: room swap in two clicks
First version was my own spreadsheet

blocks.h4: Why won't the booking platforms just build this?

blocks.p: They sell to the front desk; rosters and rooms belong to the practice manager. Different buyer, different budget line, and the booking platforms have had ten years to do it.
Built bottom-up from clinic counts in the two launch states and the price clinics named in discovery — not a top-down percentage. The working is in the data room.
Six years running operations for a four-clinic physio group. The first version of Fernroom was the spreadsheet I built there to stop Monday-morning room clashes.

ul: Sales cycle: clinics decide slowly, so pilots are 30 days with a paid conversion date set up front
Integrations: two booking systems cover most pilots; the rest export a CSV
Solo founder: the first hire is a senior engineer, budgeted in this round

blocks.h4: What does the round cost you?

blocks.p: At the $6m post-money cap, the full $600k converts to 10% of Fernroom. Post-money means every SAFE holder knows their stake the day they sign: later SAFEs in this round dilute me, not them, until the priced round.

notes.title: After each investor call
notes.body:
- Copperline: liked the pilots, wants 3 months of paid usage before deciding. Follow up @+30d.
- Pardalote: passed — too early for their fund. Offered intros to two angels; chase both this week.
- Syndicate: diligence list due @+5d — cap table, pilot contracts, usage export.
- Pattern: every call asks why the booking platforms won't build this. The answer is on the FAQ page; it gets slide 3 in deck v7.
- Tom asked whether Fernroom qualifies as an early stage innovation company. Work through the early-stage and innovation tests with the accountant before the diligence pack goes @+5d.

desks.title: Customer discovery round 2 — pricing and switching
desks.description: Twelve calls with clinic managers and owners, each scored for pain, price and fit, turned into a pricing decision before the next five pilots start.
desks.brief:
## Customer discovery, round 2 — pricing and switching

**Who** practice managers and owners at allied-health clinics
**Calls** 12 of 12 done · 25 minutes each · same script
**Round 1** 19 calls on the problem. This round tests price, and what stops a switch.

### What I needed to learn
- Will clinics pay more than the flat $149 the first pilots are on?
- Who decides — the practice manager who feels the pain, or the owner who pays?
- What would make switching from the current setup not worth it?

### What I heard
- 8 of 12 named rostering or room booking as their biggest pain
- Clinics with 8+ practitioners named $239 a month on average; smaller clinics $121
- Both not-a-fit clinics have fewer than 3 practitioners and care about invoicing, not schedules

### Decision due
Pricing for the next 5 pilots, settled before the Wattle Seed Fund meeting @+3d.

callout.title: Pricing signal: size, not discipline
callout.body: Clinics with 8+ practitioners named $239 a month on average; smaller ones $121. A flat $149 undercharges the first group and loses the second. Proposal: $129 up to 7 practitioners, $249 for 8+ — test it on the next 5 pilots.

children.label: Get both on the pilot call
3 clinics export bookings by hand weekly
Setup has to take under an hour

blocks.p: Same questions in the same order, so the answers compare. No pitching until the last five minutes.

ol: Walk me through how next week's roster got made.
When did the room schedule last go wrong? What did it cost you?
What do you use now, and what does it cost each month?
If this problem disappeared, what would you do with the time?
What would make switching not worth it?
Last five minutes: show the pilot, then ask what they would expect to pay.

ul: Ask about the last time it happened, not what usually happens
The price question comes after the walk-through, never before
Write the notes up within 10 minutes of hanging up

notes.title: Patterns so far
notes.body:
- Practice managers feel the pain; owners sign. Both need to be on the pilot call.
- 3 clinics export their bookings to a spreadsheet by hand every week — that's the import path for pilots.
- Nobody asked for more features. They want fewer phone calls on Monday morning.
- Bayview and Westgate want to start within a fortnight — send their pilot agreements first.

2. Follow up Greenhill and Calm Minds
3. Draft the two-tier pricing page

stickies.title: Don't
stickies.body: Change the price for the 4 paying pilots. Test the tiers on new clinics first.
